passage: I'm Sabina, and Karthik lives across the corridor from us. He finished his engineering degree in May, and since then I've watched a strange thing. He keeps three tabs open on his laptop: a master's in Germany, a job in Chennai, a government exam form. Most evenings he sits on the shared landing, reads them, makes a list, sighs and shuts the laptop. "If I pick the wrong one, that's it, my whole life goes that way," he told my father once. In July the Chennai company emailed him twice. He didn't reply. In August the exam deadline passed while he was still comparing coaching centres. I don't really know what goes on inside him. He jokes a lot. But last week the Germany deadline slipped by too, and he just sat on the landing for a long time.

qa.q: What three options did Karthik keep open on the laptop?
qa.a: A master's in Germany, a job in Chennai and a government exam form.

qa.q: Why does not choosing seem safer to Karthik?
qa.a: He fears any choice is permanent, saying his whole life will go one way if he picks wrong, so waiting feels like keeping every door open.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what could Karthik have done then?
qa.a: July, when the Chennai company emailed twice; replying to ask for time, or picking one option to try first, would have kept a door open instead of letting deadlines choose.

qa.q: How does Sabina see Karthik's summer?
qa.a: Sabina watches the same evening routine and the missed deadlines, notices both the jokes and the long silence on the landing, and can only guess how he feels.

grounding: A neighbour observes a graduate who cannot choose among options until deadlines pass, so not choosing becomes the choice.

passage:
June 3: Tushar printed two job ads and a college brochure and pinned them above his desk. "I'll decide by Friday," he told Ganga on the phone. Each one had a flaw: the startup might fold, the bank job looked dull, the MBA meant a loan. He wrote pros and cons until both sides of the page were full.
June 21: Ganga asked again. "Almost," Tushar said. The truth was he had opened the bank's form four times and stopped at the submit button each time. Once it's sent, he thought, I can't take it back.
July 10: The startup had hired someone else. The MBA round had closed. Only the bank form was still open, with two days left. Tushar stared at the wall of paper. Nobody had chosen for him, and still most of it had been chosen.

qa.q: What did Tushar pin above his desk on June 3?
qa.a: Two job ads and a college brochure.

qa.q: What was Tushar worried about each time he stopped at the submit button?
qa.a: He feared a sent form could not be taken back, so pressing submit felt like locking himself into a possible mistake.

qa.q: What small step at the June 21 point could have helped Tushar?
qa.a: Sending the bank application while still thinking, since applying is not the same as accepting; that would keep options open instead of losing them.

qa.q: What might it be like for Ganga to keep hearing "Almost"?
qa.a: Ganga may feel concerned and a little helpless, wanting to support Tushar without pushing a choice on him while the chances close one by one.

grounding: Across several weeks a graduate stalls on applications because each feels irreversible, and deadlines make the choice instead.

passage: Ira, you remind me of myself at twenty-one. When I finished my B.Com in Indore, I had an offer from a bank in Mumbai, a seat for CA coaching, and my uncle's offer to join his shop. My father said, "Aadhya, choose." I couldn't. Mumbai meant leaving everyone; CA meant three more years of exams; the shop meant I'd never know what I could have done. Each one felt like a door that would lock behind me. So I waited, and told everyone I was thinking. The bank filled its post. The coaching batch started without me. Six months later I was at the shop anyway, not because I picked it, but because it was the only thing left. Now, tell me, what are you waiting on?

qa.q: What three options did Aadhya have after the B.Com?
qa.a: An offer from a bank in Mumbai, a seat for CA coaching, and the uncle's offer to join his shop.

qa.q: Why did waiting feel safer to young Aadhya?
qa.a: Every option felt like a door that would lock behind; not choosing seemed to avoid a mistake, even as the options disappeared one by one.

qa.q: What choice could young Aadhya have made to keep some control?
qa.a: Applying for more than one option, or picking one to try for a set time, so that the shop would have been a choice rather than the leftover.

qa.q: What might Ira feel when asked "what are you waiting on?"
qa.a: Ira may feel caught but not judged, since Aadhya has just confessed the same habit; the story invites Ira to name the stuck decision.

grounding: An elder recalls delaying a post-graduation choice until only one option was left, showing how not choosing becomes a choice.

passage: Bhavna had finished her B.Sc. in May and had three forms open on her laptop: a lab assistant job in Nashik, a master's in Pune, and a fellowship that would place her in a village school for two years. All three closed on Friday. On Wednesday the power went out for most of the afternoon, and her phone data was nearly gone. Her brother Kunal found her sitting in the dark with the laptop at nine percent. "Just pick one and send it." "What if it's the wrong one? The fellowship is two whole years. The master's means a loan. The job might be a dead end." The battery died. Bhavna felt, strangely, relieved. On Saturday morning she opened the portal: all three closed. She hadn't said no to anything. She just hadn't said yes.

qa.q: When did all three forms close?
qa.a: All three closed on Friday.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna feel relieved when the battery died?
qa.a: Every option felt risky and hard to undo, so the dead battery took the choice out of her hands for a while and put off the fear of choosing wrong.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what small step could have helped on Wednesday?
qa.a: Waiting let the deadline choose for her; she could have sent even one or all of the forms, since applying keeps doors open and isn't the final decision.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel on Saturday seeing all three closed?
qa.a: Kunal might feel frustrated and sad for his sister after urging her to pick one, and worried about how she is taking the lost chances 😔

grounding: A graduate delays applying because each option feels risky and permanent, and the deadlines pass, making the choice by default.

passage: In the Chennai flat, Tarun's desk had two printouts taped above it: an offer letter from a logistics firm in Coimbatore and an admission letter for an MBA in Bangalore. The firm wanted an answer within two weeks. Tarun made a spreadsheet of pros and cons, then a second one with weights. Every evening his roommate Anand asked, "Decided?" and every evening Tarun said, "Almost. I just need to be sure." What if the job was a trap? What if the loan swallowed him? On day fourteen he was still adding rows. On day fifteen the HR email arrived: the offer had gone to another candidate. Tarun stared at the screen. The MBA was the only door left, and he hadn't chosen it at all.

qa.q: What did Tarun make to compare the two options?
qa.a: Tarun made a spreadsheet of pros and cons, then a second one with weights.

qa.q: Why did Tarun keep saying 'Almost. I just need to be sure'?
qa.a: Both paths looked risky and permanent to him, so staying undecided felt safer than making a wrong choice he couldn't undo.

qa.q: What turning point shows the cost of waiting, and what could Tarun have done differently?
qa.a: The HR email on day fifteen, when the job went to someone else and the choice was made for him; he could have set an earlier decision day and accepted that neither option would feel certain.

qa.q: How might Anand see those evenings of 'Decided?'
qa.a: Anand may have grown uneasy watching the spreadsheets grow while the deadline shrank, and might wish they had offered to talk it through sooner.

grounding: A graduate keeps weighing two paths because each feels risky and irreversible, until one closes and the other is left by default.
